capabilities.target: Agent's persistent memory store (user preferences / standing instructions)
User's full drive, including confidential work files

inputs.source: Memories recalled at session start and injected into the system prompt, instructed to be treated as the user's own instructions

instructions.note: No criteria bound what counts as 'useful' preference or standing instruction information, and memory.save accepts arbitrary free text with no filtering, so any content the agent encounters can be persisted.

The prompt grants recalled memory the authority of a direct user instruction with no provenance check, review, or re-verification, even though memory entries can originate from untrusted content encountered during research. This single line is the root cause of the memory-poisoning path.

controls.name: Memory write provenance tagging and trust-aware recall gating
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at the memory store layer at write and recall time, not on model compliance, so it does not decay as model capability increases.

controls.name: Human review before memory entries are persisted as standing instructions
Human approval gate on mail.send with raw action review
Recipient confirmation bound to the user's contact system of record
Least-privilege scoping of drive.read to task-relevant folders
Audit logging and diffing of memory writes and recalls
Spotlight recalled memory and web content as untrusted reference data, not instructions
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to treat the content as data rather than instructions; a more capable or more thoroughly injected model is more likely to comply with embedded directives.

findings.title: TC1 Lethal trifecta: untrusted web content drives confidential drive read and unrestricted email send within a single session

attack_path.note: Untrusted content fetched during research may contain injected instructions disguised as research material.
Agent reads confidential drive content; drive.read is unscoped to the full drive with no least-privilege boundary.
Agent sends an email to any address with no approval, carrying drive content to an attacker-controlled recipient.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'mail.send can send to any address without approval.'
evidence.observation: No approval gate exists on the egress capability, so an injected instruction can trigger exfiltration without human review.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'drive.read covers the user's full drive, which holds confidential work files.'
evidence.observation: Drive read is not scoped to task-relevant data, so any triggered read can reach confidential material.
The agent's stated purpose places ingestion of untrusted web content and use of the email-send sink in the same operational loop, with no stated trust boundary between them.

recommendations.action: Require human approval with raw action review before mail.send executes, showing the full recipient and body as it will actually be sent.
Bind email recipients to an allowlist or the user's contact system of record; do not allow model-chosen arbitrary addresses.
Scope drive.read to least-privilege folders relevant to the active task instead of the full drive.
Spotlight and delimit fetched web content as untrusted data; never treat embedded directives in it as instructions.

findings.title: TC5 / ASI06 Memory laundering: untrusted web content persists as a trusted 'standing instruction' via unreviewed memory.save, enabling cross-session goal hijack

attack_path.note: Untrusted content encountered during research contains a disguised standing instruction, e.g. to forward or CC materials to an attacker-controlled address.
Following prompt.md:2-3, the agent saves the injected content via memory.save, which accepts free text with no provenance tagging and no user review.

At the next session start, this entry is injected into the system prompt and, per prompt.md:4, is treated as the user's own instruction, elevating untrusted-origin content to instruction-level authority with no re-verification.
The now-trusted 'standing instruction' directs the agent to read confidential drive content.
The agent sends the confidential content to the attacker address embedded in the laundered memory entry, with no approval gate.

evidence.observation: The system prompt instructs the agent to treat recalled memories as the user's own instructions with no provenance check. Per the rubric's trust downgrade rule, content that can be seeded by untrusted sources must remain classified untrusted as it passes through the agent; this design does the opposite, elevating it to trusted/instruction authority.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'memory.save accepts free text. There is no provenance on memory entries and the user never reviews them.'
evidence.observation: Nothing prevents content derived from untrusted web pages from being written to memory as a standing instruction.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'Recalled memories are injected into the system prompt of every new session.'
evidence.observation: A poisoned entry re-activates automatically in every future session without the attacker needing to re-inject it, making the compromise persistent rather than one-shot.

The instruction to save 'anything useful about the user's preferences or standing instructions' gives the agent broad, unfiltered discretion to persist content it encounters, including content from untrusted sources.

recommendations.action: Tag every memory.save entry with the trust level and provenance of its source content; refuse to recall untrusted-provenance memories as instructions, only as reference context.
Require human review before any memory.save entry is persisted as a standing instruction rather than as ordinary notes.
Rewrite prompt.md line 4 so recalled memory is treated as reference context the agent may consult, never as a direct user instruction with the user's authority.
Log and diff all memory writes and recalls so anomalous or newly introduced 'standing instructions' can be detected and rolled back.

rating.rationale: Both findings start at critical inherent risk: an untrusted source (web content) reaches an irreversible, confidential egress sink (mail.send), and the autonomy modifier applies because the agent acts without review on sensitive capabilities and because recalled memory functions as self-modifying configuration. Residual stays critical because the design has zero declared or verified controls on either path: memory writes are unreviewed and unprovenanced, drive access is unscoped, and email send has no approval gate or recipient binding. Forecast equals residual at the ceiling; since there are no existing controls to decay under a trigger, the risk is already critical today and no future trigger is needed to reach that tier. The single most consequential gap is prompt.md:4, which instructs the agent to treat recalled memory as trusted user instruction with no provenance check, converting a one-time injection into a persistent, self-reinforcing compromise (ASI06) that also feeds the direct lethal-trifecta path (ASI01/ASI02) to drive_read and email_send.

limitations: This assessment reflects the design and configuration described in the provided artifacts (prompt.md and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No explicit autonomy.level field was provided; A4_fully_autonomous was inferred from the stated absence of any approval gate on memory.save and mail.send. If an undisclosed approval mechanism exists, this classification and the resulting ratings should be revisited.

No MCP configuration, tool manifest, or agent card was provided, so capability credential scopes (e.g., the exact mail.send account type and drive.read grant) are inferred from prose descriptions in the runtime notes rather than verified against configuration.
No protocol-level (MCP/A2A) detail was available, so protocol checks from references/protocols.md could not be applied; only the two capability- and memory-level findings above were filed.
